0026e2f891f5b5: Why "I didn't know" almost never protects you legally, and why that makes learning this urgent, not optional.
1b615a0e494376:
An uncomfortable reality

Almost every legal system in the world has a harsh principle: "ignorance of the law is no excuse." Not being able to claim "I didn't know" is the rule, not the exception. That means, whether you like it or not, understanding at least the basics of your rights and obligations isn't curiosity — it's a practical necessity.

Why no one taught you this

Formal education rarely includes a real course on "how the legal system around you works" — you learn history, math, literature, but almost never how to defend yourself if you're detained without cause, how an employment contract works, or where to go if one of your rights is violated. That gap isn't an accident in many places: people who don't know their rights are easier to ignore.

⚠️ You can't rely only on someone else explaining it to you once it's already urgent. By the time you need to know your rights against the police, your employer, or a hospital, it's too late to start researching from scratch — you need the foundation before the situation happens.

What this course IS, and what it's NOT

  • ✅ It is: a general map of how legal systems work, and the most important categories of rights.
  • ✅ It is: the starting point for knowing when you need real professional help.
  • ❌ It is not: legal advice for your personal case — laws change by country, state/province, and over time.
  • ❌ It is not: a substitute for a lawyer if you have a real legal situation.
💡 This course gives you the conceptual foundation. The "My Rights as a Mexican" and "My Rights as a Canadian" courses (with more countries to be added over time) apply this to a specific country.

1b8afa76b90c48: What is a law? The hierarchy of norms
0b6f19765b5a8f: Why not all rules carry the same weight — from the constitution down to a simple municipal ordinance.
1f78fb6f8fca24:
Not all rules carry the same weight

Almost every country has a hierarchy of norms — an order of importance among different types of rules. Understanding this hierarchy helps you understand why certain laws can be declared invalid.

The typical pyramid

  1. Constitution: the country's supreme rule. All other laws must be consistent with it. It usually contains the fundamental rights.
  2. International treaties: in many countries, international agreements that have been signed and ratified rank very high, sometimes on par with the constitution.
  3. Federal/national laws: passed by the whole country's legislative branch.
  4. State/provincial laws: in countries with a federal system, each state or province can legislate on certain topics.
  5. Regulations and municipal ordinances: more specific, local rules, at the lowest level of the pyramid.
🏛️ Why the order matters: if a municipal ordinance contradicts a federal law, or a law contradicts the constitution, that rule can be declared invalid by a court — the highest level always wins.

The three branches

Most modern democracies split the power of the State into three branches to prevent any single one from having too much control:

  • Legislative branch: creates the laws (congress, parliament).
  • Executive branch: applies them and administers the country (president, government).
  • Judicial branch: interprets the laws and resolves conflicts (courts, tribunals).
💡 When you hear that a law was "declared unconstitutional" by a court, now you know exactly what that means: a court determined that law violates the rule at the top of the pyramid.

08fd615dbda602:
Two ways to build a legal system

Most countries in the world follow, with variations, one of these two major legal traditions:

Civil law (Roman-Germanic tradition)

Predominant in Latin America (including Mexico), continental Europe, and much of the world. It's based on comprehensive written codes that try to anticipate most possible situations. Judges apply the code to the facts of the case; their earlier decisions don't formally bind future cases to be decided the same way.

Common law

Predominant in the United Kingdom, the United States, and Canada (except Quebec, which uses civil law for private matters). It relies heavily on judicial precedent: decisions from earlier courts in similar cases carry binding force for future cases — the system is built case by case, not only by written code.

⚖️ A practical difference: in Mexico, a judge first looks at what the relevant code (civil, criminal, etc.) says. In Canada (outside Quebec), a lawyer also researches what earlier courts decided in similar cases, because those decisions can be as important as the written law itself.

Why this matters to you

This difference isn't just academic: it explains why the process for claiming a right, filing a lawsuit, or understanding a court ruling feels different between countries that at first glance seem similar.

💡 In the upcoming courses in this same track you'll see this in action: Mexico (civil/codified law) and Canada (common law in most provinces) organize their legal protections in structurally different ways.

16bbac80c43d07: Why human rights are considered different from other legal rights — and the international document that formalized them after World War II.
11891a88b3bf8a:
A different kind of right

Human rights are considered conceptually different from other legal rights: they don't depend on a government "granting" them — the idea is that they belong to every person simply by being one, and States have an obligation to recognize and protect them, not to grant them as a favor.

The 1948 Universal Declaration

After the devastation of World War II, the newly created United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948 — a 30-article document that sought to establish an internationally recognized minimum floor of human dignity, after the world had witnessed just how far its absence could go.

📜 Some of its most cited articles: the right to life and liberty (Art. 3), prohibition of torture (Art. 5), equality before the law (Art. 7), the right to a fair trial (Art. 10), freedom of expression (Art. 19), the right to education (Art. 26).

From declaration to real legal obligation

The 1948 Declaration isn't, by itself, legally binding — it's a declaration of principles. But international treaties were built from it that do generate real legal obligations for the countries that sign and ratify them, and many national constitutions (including Mexico's and Canada's) incorporate these principles directly into their own legal text.

💡 When you see phrases like "human rights recognized in the Constitution" in the following courses, now you know where that tradition comes from: a deliberate international effort to make "never again" more than just a phrase.

08ad133e70e742: The difference between a civil conflict and a criminal offense, and the minimum guarantees almost every serious legal system promises anyone who's accused.
07294213a5b45d:
Two very different types of conflict

Civil law (not to be confused with the legal tradition from class 3)

Resolves conflicts between private parties: a breached contract, a divorce, a property dispute, a damages lawsuit. The State acts as a neutral referee between two private parties. The typical outcome is financial compensation or an order to do/stop doing something.

Criminal law

Resolves conflicts where the State itself accuses a person of having committed a crime against society (theft, fraud, assault). The outcome can include prison, fines, or other penalties — which is why the protections for the accused are much stricter than in a civil case.

Due process: nearly universal guarantees

Almost every serious legal system promises, at least in principle, these protections to anyone accused of a crime:

  • Presumption of innocence: you're considered innocent until proven otherwise, not the other way around.
  • Right to be clearly informed of the accusation against you.
  • Right to legal defense — including free defense if you can't afford a lawyer.
  • Right to remain silent without that being used as proof of guilt.
  • Right to a trial before an impartial authority, within a reasonable time.
⚠️ These guarantees EXISTING in the law doesn't mean they're always respected in practice everywhere — but knowing they exist is the first step toward demanding they be upheld if you ever need them.
💡 In the country-specific courses you'll see these guarantees under specific names and details (for example, "Miranda rights" in the Anglo-American context, or the guarantees of Article 20 of the Constitution in Mexico).

196a944a29126a: The most practical module in the course: what kinds of help exist, what they're called, and how to tell when you can handle something yourself and when you need a professional.
0560a09dea3a3e:
Not everything requires an expensive private lawyer

One of the most costly myths is believing the only option for resolving a legal problem is hiring a private lawyer. Most countries have alternatives, some of them completely free.

Types of legal help that usually exist

  • Public defender's office / free legal aid: lawyers paid by the State for people who can't afford a private one, especially in criminal cases.
  • Human rights commissions: agencies (often government-run but autonomous) that receive complaints about human rights violations by authorities.
  • Consumer protection agencies: for conflicts with companies, defective products, improper charges.
  • Unions and labor conciliation boards: for conflicts between workers and employers.
  • Specialized nongovernmental organizations (NGOs): many offer free legal guidance on specific issues (immigration, housing, gender-based violence).
  • University legal clinics: advanced law students, supervised by professors, offering free or low-cost advice at many universities.

How to know what kind of help you need

🧭 Guiding questions:
  • Is it a conflict with another person or company (civil), or are you accused of a crime (criminal)? — determines whether you need a public defender or civil mediation.
  • Is it urgent (an arrest, an imminent eviction) or can it wait a few days of research?
  • Does the amount or seriousness of the matter justify paying a private lawyer, or is there a reasonable free path?
⚠️ This course gives you the general map — the country-specific courses in this same school include the real names of these institutions in Mexico and Canada, so you know exactly who to look for.

What you covered

You started by understanding why knowing your rights is your own responsibility, not an optional luxury (class 1). You saw the hierarchy of norms and the three branches of the State (class 2), the world's two major legal traditions (class 3), the origin of modern human rights (class 4), how a judicial process and its minimum guarantees work (class 5), and where to actually go if you need help (class 6).

This course was the map, not the territory

Everything you saw here is general — it applies, with variations, to most democratic legal systems in the world. But your concrete rights depend on the specific country and state/province where you live. That's why Oliver Academy's Law School is organized by country: this course is the conceptual foundation, and the ones that follow are the real application to your context.

⚠️ Always remember the honest limit of courses like this: they're general civic education, not legal advice for your personal case. Laws change, vary by place, and a real lawyer or official institution will always be able to give you a more precise answer than any course.
💡 But now you have something a lot of people never had the chance to formally learn: the general map so you don't depend entirely on others when it comes to your own rights.
